chapters.title: 한글
chapters.summary: Read and write the Korean alphabet, from single vowels to final consonants.
chapters.culture: Hangeul was created in 1443 and published in 1446. Its consonant shapes come from the mouth, tongue, and throat, which is why the alphabet can be learned quickly.

lessons.title: 한글을 배워요 ①
lessons.summary: Six basic vowels, ten basic consonants, and the shape of one syllable block.
goals: Read and write ㅏ ㅓ ㅗ ㅜ ㅡ ㅣ
Recognise ㄱ ㄴ ㄷ ㄹ ㅁ ㅂ ㅅ ㅇ ㅈ ㅎ
Combine a consonant and a vowel into one syllable

grammar.title: Three shapes build every vowel
grammar.explanation: Korean vowels are drawn from heaven (a round dot), earth (a flat line), and a person (a vertical line). The position of the dot changes the sound. ㅏ opens the mouth wide, ㅓ is deeper, ㅗ is rounded, ㅜ is rounded with the lips forward, ㅡ is flat, and ㅣ is a clear ee sound.
grammar.tip: The dot belongs on the right of ㅏ and on the left of ㅓ. Moving it changes the vowel completely.

grammar.title: Ten basic consonants
grammar.pattern: ㄱ ㄴ ㄷ ㄹ ㅁ ㅂ ㅅ ㅇ ㅈ ㅎ
grammar.explanation: Each basic consonant imitates a speech organ: ㄱ the back of the tongue, ㄴ the tongue tip, ㅁ the lips, ㅅ the teeth, and ㅇ the throat. The remaining letters add strokes to those five shapes.

examples.english: a light k released into ah

grammar.tip: At the start of a syllable, ㅇ is silent. It holds the vowel when there is no consonant sound.

grammar.title: One block, one syllable
grammar.explanation: Korean is written in square blocks. A consonant sits on the left or top, and a vowel sits on the right or below. Each block is read as one syllable, left to right and top to bottom.
grammar.tip: Vowels with a vertical line stand to the right of the consonant. Vowels with a horizontal line sit below it.

practice.prompt: Which vowel is open and bright: ㅏ or ㅓ?
practice.answer: ㅏ. It is written with the dot on the right of the vertical line.

practice.prompt: Read the block 가.
practice.answer: A light k released into an open ah.

practice.prompt: Build 마 from its two parts.

lessons.culture: Korean is written in syllable blocks rather than a straight line of letters, so a short word can look like a small square.

lessons.title: 한글을 배워요 ②
lessons.summary: Tense consonants, aspirated consonants, and the compound vowels.
goals: Hear the difference between ㄲ and ㅋ
Read the tense and aspirated consonant sets
Recognise the compound vowels built from ㅑ ㅕ ㅛ ㅠ

grammar.title: Tense consonants
grammar.explanation: Tense consonants are made with a tight throat and no puff of air. English speakers often hear them as stronger versions of the plain letters. In Korean they are separate sounds and can change a word.

examples.english: older brother, said by a younger woman
seed, or a polite name suffix

grammar.tip: Put your hand in front of your mouth. A tense sound should move almost no air.

grammar.title: Aspirated consonants
grammar.explanation: Aspirated consonants carry a strong puff of air. They are the breathy partners of ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, and ㅈ. The puff is the point of the sound, so do not hold it back.
grammar.tip: A sheet of paper held in front of your lips should move when you say ㅋ, ㅌ, ㅍ, or ㅊ.

grammar.title: Compound vowels
grammar.pattern: ㅑ ㅕ ㅛ ㅠ · ㅘ ㅝ ㅟ ㅢ · ㅒ ㅖ ㅚ ㅙ ㅞ
grammar.explanation: Compound vowels begin with one sound and glide into another. The ㅑ family adds a y-glide to the basic vowels. The ㅘ family glides from a rounded o or u. The ㅒ family glides from a bright e.

examples.english: a flat uh gliding into ee

grammar.tip: Say the first sound, then let your mouth move into the second. Do not split the vowel into two syllables.

practice.prompt: Which consonant is tense: ㅋ or ㄲ?
practice.answer: ㄲ. The tense sound is tight and has almost no puff of air.

practice.prompt: Read 토끼.
practice.answer: An aspirated t, a rounded oh, a tense k, and ee: the word for rabbit.

practice.prompt: Which vowel has a y-glide: ㅏ or ㅑ?

lessons.culture: Korean treats tight and breathy consonants as different letters. A learner who hears them as one sound will struggle with pairs such as ㄲ and ㅋ.

lessons.title: 한글을 배워요 ③
lessons.summary: Final consonants, double finals, and the liaison that carries a sound into the next syllable.
goals: Read a syllable with a final consonant
Reduce a double final to one sound
Link a final consonant to a following vowel

grammar.title: Final consonants
grammar.explanation: A consonant at the bottom of a syllable is called 받침. It closes the syllable. Korean reduces many written finals to seven representative sounds: ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, and ㅇ.
grammar.tip: Do not add a vowel after the final. Stop the sound cleanly at the consonant.

grammar.title: Double finals
grammar.pattern: ㄳ ㄵ ㄺ ㄻ ㄼ ㅄ
grammar.explanation: Some syllables carry two written consonants at the bottom. Only one is pronounced in the plain form; the other appears when the next syllable begins with a vowel.

examples.english: the ㄴ is carried into the next syllable
the ㅂ sound carries into a tense ss

grammar.tip: Learn double finals as a pair: one sound now, the other sound when a vowel follows.

grammar.title: Liaison
grammar.explanation: When a syllable ends in a consonant and the next syllable begins with ㅇ, the final consonant moves into the empty initial position. This is why written boundaries and spoken syllables do not always match.
grammar.tip: Liaison is normal speech, not a shortcut. Practise it slowly, then let it flow.

practice.prompt: Which seven sounds represent final consonants?
practice.answer: ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, and ㅇ.

practice.prompt: How does 밥을 sound?
practice.answer: 바블, because the final ㅂ moves into the next syllable.

practice.prompt: Read 값.
practice.answer: A closed b final, even though two consonants are written.

lessons.culture: Korean children learn 받침 as part of every syllable, so the final consonant is never an afterthought. Clean finals make speech easier to follow.

chapters.title: 소개
chapters.summary: Greet people, give your name, and talk about nationality and family.
chapters.culture: A first meeting in Korea often begins with a small bow and a clear name. Asking about work or nationality is a normal way to find a shared topic.

lessons.title: 만나서 반갑습니다
lessons.summary: Formal polite greetings, the subject marker, and the formal copula.
goals: Greet someone in a formal setting
Use -ㅂ니다/습니다 and -ㅂ니까?/습니까?
Mark the subject with 이/가
Say what someone is with 입니다

vocabulary.english: Mr, Ms, a polite suffix after a name

grammar.title: Formal polite present
grammar.explanation: Add ㅂ니다 after a vowel stem and 습니다 after a consonant stem. This ending is used in meetings, presentations, announcements, and careful first conversations. The question form replaces 다 with 까.
grammar.tip: This is not old-fashioned speech. It is the safe choice when you are unsure how close you are to the listener. Stems ending in ㄹ drop it before ㅂ니다: 살다 → 삽니다.

grammar.title: Subject marker 이/가
grammar.explanation: 이/가 marks the subject of a sentence. Use 이 after a final consonant and 가 after a vowel. It often introduces new information or points to who or what does something.
grammar.tip: 누구 becomes 누가 when it takes the subject marker.

grammar.title: The formal copula
grammar.explanation: 입니다 links a noun to another noun in formal polite speech. It means is, am, or are. The question form is 입니까? The ending does not change for a final consonant.
grammar.tip: Do not add 이/가 to the noun before 입니다 unless the sentence needs a subject marker for emphasis.

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.english: Hello. I am Minho.

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: Hello. I am Jane. Nice to meet you.

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.english: Yes, nice to meet you too.

practice.prompt: Complete formally: 저는 학생__.
Ask formally: Are you a teacher?
Choose 이 or 가: 물__ 차갑습니다.
practice.answer: 이, because 물 ends in a consonant.

lessons.culture: In a formal introduction, say your name slowly and clearly. A small bow and both hands on a business card are common when meeting someone older or in business.

lessons.title: 저는 제인입니다
lessons.summary: Talk about nationality and jobs with the topic marker and the negative copula.
goals: Use 은/는 to set the topic
Ask which one with 어느
Say what you are not with 이/가 아닙니다

grammar.title: Topic marker 은/는
grammar.explanation: 은/는 sets the topic of the sentence: as for this person or thing. Use 은 after a consonant and 는 after a vowel. It can also contrast two topics.

examples.english: As for me, I am a student.

grammar.tip: 이/가 points to the subject; 은/는 frames the topic. A sentence can contain both.

grammar.title: Which one: 어느
grammar.explanation: 어느 asks which one among a known set. It comes directly before the noun.
grammar.tip: 무슨 asks what kind; 어느 asks which one of a group.

grammar.title: Negative copula
grammar.explanation: To say that something is not a certain noun, add 이 아닙니다 after a consonant or 가 아닙니다 after a vowel.
grammar.tip: The negative copula is a full phrase: 이/가 + 아닙니다. Do not write 이/가 안 입니다.

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: I am Jane. I am American.

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.korean: 아, 그래요? 저는 민호입니다. 한국 사람입니다.
dialogue.english: Oh, really? I am Minho. I am Korean.

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: Minho, are you a student?

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.english: No, I am not a student. I am an office worker.

practice.prompt: Choose 은 or 는: 저__ 학생입니다.
practice.answer: 는, because 저 ends in a vowel.

practice.prompt: Say: I am not a doctor.
Ask: Which country are you from?

lessons.culture: Korean conversations often establish nationality and occupation early. A simple answer with one detail is enough; long self-descriptions can feel formal.

lessons.title: 이 사람은 누구예요?
lessons.summary: Introduce family and friends with the informal polite copula.
goals: Use 이에요/예요 in friendly conversation
Say what someone is not with 아니에요
Ask who someone is

grammar.title: Informal polite copula
grammar.explanation: 이에요/예요 is the everyday polite version of 입니다. Use 이에요 after a consonant and 예요 after a vowel. The question form uses the same ending with a rising tone.
grammar.tip: After a vowel, write 예요. 의사 + 예요 becomes 의사예요; after a consonant, 학생 + 이에요 becomes 학생이에요.

grammar.title: Informal negative copula
grammar.explanation: Use 이 아니에요 after a consonant and 가 아니에요 after a vowel to say that something is not a certain noun.

examples.english: My younger sibling is not a student.

grammar.tip: This is the friendly match for 이/가 아닙니다.

grammar.title: Who: 누구
grammar.explanation: 누구 means who. As a subject it becomes 누가. It can also follow a topic marker: 이 사람은 누구예요?
grammar.tip: 누구 + 이/가 contracts to 누가. Do not say 누구가.

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: Who is this person?

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.english: She is my friend. Her name is Yuki.

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: Yuki, are you a student?

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.english: No, she is not a student. She is a teacher.

practice.prompt: Choose 이에요 or 예요: 저는 학생__.
practice.answer: 이에요, because 학생 ends in a consonant.

practice.prompt: Say: I am not a doctor. (friendly polite)
Ask: Who is this person?

lessons.culture: When introducing someone, give the relationship first and the name second: 제 친구예요, 유키예요. It sounds warmer than starting with the name.

chapters.title: 시간과 날짜
chapters.summary: Talk about daily routines, dates, and what happened over the weekend.
chapters.culture: Korean dates run year, month, day. Many traditional holidays follow the lunar calendar, so their Gregorian dates change each year.

lessons.title: 몇 시에 일어나요?
lessons.englishTitle: What time do you get up?
lessons.summary: Daily routines with the object marker, time particle, and polite informal present.
goals: Mark an object with 을/를
Say when something happens with 에
Use -아요/어요 in everyday speech

grammar.title: Object marker 을/를
grammar.explanation: 을/를 marks the object of an action. Use 을 after a final consonant and 를 after a vowel. In casual speech it is often dropped.
grammar.tip: Do not put 을/를 on the subject. If the noun is doing the action, use 이/가 or 은/는.

grammar.title: Time particle 에
grammar.explanation: 에 marks the time when something happens. It attaches to clock times, days, months, and years. Do not use it with 어제, 오늘, 내일, or 언제.

examples.english: I get up in the morning.
I go to school on Monday.

grammar.tip: 오늘, 어제, 내일, and 언제 never take 에.

grammar.title: Polite informal present
grammar.explanation: This is the everyday polite ending. After ㅏ or ㅗ use 아요; after other vowels use 어요; 하다 verbs become 해요. It is friendly but still polite.
grammar.tip: When the stem already ends in the same vowel, the sounds merge: 가 + 아요 → 가요.

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.english: Jane, what time do you get up?

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: I get up at seven in the morning.

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.english: What do you do in the morning?

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: I eat breakfast. Then I go to school.

practice.prompt: Choose 을 or 를: 밥__ 먹어요.
practice.answer: 을, because 밥 ends in a consonant.

practice.prompt: Add the time particle: 아침__ 일어나요.
Change to polite informal: 공부하다.

lessons.culture: School and work days often start early in Korea, so 몇 시에 일어나요? is a common small-talk question. The answer usually includes a time and one morning habit.

lessons.title: 오늘이 몇 월 며칠이에요?
lessons.summary: Dates, weekdays, from-to ranges, and polite negation with -지 않다.
goals: Say months, days, and weekdays
Use 부터 and 까지 for a range
Negate a verb with -지 않다

grammar.title: From to
grammar.explanation: 부터 marks the start of a time range and 까지 marks the end. They can attach to days, dates, or clock times.

examples.english: I study from Monday to Friday.

examples.korean: 아홉 시부터 열두 시까지 수업이 있어요.
examples.english: I have class from nine to twelve.

grammar.tip: The order is start부터 end까지. Do not reverse them.

grammar.title: What kind: 무슨
grammar.explanation: 무슨 asks what kind of thing something is. It comes before the noun, like an adjective.

examples.english: What day of the week is it?
What kind of book are you reading?

grammar.tip: 몇 asks a number; 무슨 asks a kind.

grammar.title: Polite negation
grammar.explanation: Add -지 않다 to a verb or adjective stem to say that something does not happen or is not the case. In casual speech, 안 before the verb can replace it.
grammar.tip: Do not use -지 않다 in commands or suggestions. For “don't do it”, use -지 마세요.

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: What is the date today?

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.english: It is October 21st.

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: What day of the week is it?

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.english: It is Wednesday.

practice.prompt: Say: from Monday to Friday.
Choose 무슨 or 몇: __ 요일이에요?
Negate politely: 오늘은 공부해요.

lessons.culture: Korean date order is year, month, day, and the month name often uses a native number: 시월 for October. Listening for the month first helps you follow announcements.
reference: KGIU Beginning · time and date expressions

lessons.title: 주말에 무엇을 했어요?
lessons.englishTitle: What did you do on the weekend?
lessons.summary: Tell a short weekend story with the past tense and sequence connectors.
goals: Connect two actions with -고
Say after doing something with -(으)ㄴ 후에
Use the polite past tense -았어요/었어요

grammar.title: Connecting actions
grammar.explanation: -고 connects two actions in order or adds one action to another. The tense is shown on the final verb.

examples.english: I met a friend and watched a movie.
I ate and then took a walk.

grammar.tip: -고 can also mean and without a strict time order. Context decides.

grammar.title: After doing
grammar.explanation: Add -은 후에 after a consonant stem and -ㄴ 후에 after a vowel stem. It means after doing something. The tense appears on the second clause.

examples.english: After doing homework, I watched a movie.
After eating, I took a walk.

grammar.tip: 후에 can be replaced by 뒤에 or 다음에 without changing the meaning.

grammar.title: Polite past tense
grammar.explanation: After ㅏ or ㅗ use 았어요; after other vowels use 었어요; 하다 verbs become 했어요. This is the everyday polite past.
grammar.tip: The past ending attaches to the stem, then the polite 요 is added.

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.english: What did you do on the weekend?

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: I met a friend and watched a movie.

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.english: Was the movie interesting?

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: Yes, it was very interesting.

practice.prompt: Connect: 친구를 만났어요. + 영화를 봤어요.
Say: After doing homework, I took a walk.
Change to past: 공부해요.

lessons.culture: Monday small talk often starts with the weekend. A two-part answer, one activity plus one detail, sounds natural and keeps the conversation moving.

chapters.title: 위치와 장소
chapters.summary: Describe where things are, what happens in a place, and how to get somewhere.
chapters.culture: Korean directions often use landmarks rather than street names. A bank, a hospital, or a convenience store is a more useful anchor than a road number.

lessons.title: 가방 안에 책과 공책이 있어요
lessons.englishTitle: There is a book and a notebook in the bag
lessons.summary: Existence, position nouns, and joining two things with 와/과.
goals: Say that something exists or does not exist
Place an object with 에
Join two nouns with 와/과

grammar.title: Existence
grammar.explanation: 있다 means to exist or to have; 없다 means not to exist or not to have. The thing that exists takes 이/가.
grammar.tip: The possessed thing is the subject, so it takes 이/가, not 을/를.

grammar.title: Location particle 에
grammar.explanation: 에 marks where something exists when used with 있다 or 없다. Position nouns such as 안, 위, 아래, 앞, and 뒤 come before 에.

examples.english: There is a book in the bag.
There is a notebook on the desk.
There is no bag under the chair.

grammar.tip: 에 marks existence here. 에서 marks where an action happens.

grammar.title: Joining nouns
grammar.explanation: 와/과 means and between nouns. Use 과 after a consonant and 와 after a vowel. In casual speech 하고 or 랑 can replace it.
grammar.tip: 와/과 joins nouns only. To join sentences, use -고.

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: What is in the bag?

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.english: There are a book and a notebook.

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: Is there a book on the desk too?

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.english: No, there is not one on the desk.

practice.prompt: Say: There is a book in the bag.
Choose 와 or 과: 책__ 공책.
practice.answer: 과, because 책 ends in a consonant.

practice.prompt: Say: I do not have time.

lessons.culture: Many Korean homes have heated floors, so people often sit and sleep on the floor. Position words such as 위 and 아래 describe everyday comfort, not just geometry.

lessons.title: 도서관에서 공부를 해요
lessons.summary: Action locations, before doing something, and short negation with 안.
goals: Say where an action happens with 에서
Say before doing something with -기 전에
Negate a verb with 안

grammar.title: Where an action happens
grammar.explanation: 에서 marks the place where an action takes place. It is different from 에, which marks where something exists.
grammar.tip: If the verb is 있다/없다, use 에. For actions such as 공부하다 or 먹다, use 에서.

grammar.title: Before doing
grammar.explanation: -기 전에 means before doing something. The tense is carried by the second clause, not by the -기 form.

examples.english: I wash my hands before eating.
I went to the library before class ended.

grammar.tip: Do not add a past tense to the -기 clause: 먹었기 전에 is wrong.

grammar.title: Short negation with 안
grammar.explanation: Put 안 before a verb or adjective to negate it in everyday speech. It has the same meaning as -지 않다 but is shorter.
grammar.tip: 안 goes before the verb, not before the object: 커피를 안 마셔요 is correct.

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.english: Where are you now?

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: I am studying in the library.

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.english: What did you do before studying?

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: I met a friend at a coffee shop.

practice.prompt: Choose 에 or 에서: 도서관__ 공부해요.
practice.answer: 에서, because 공부하다 is an action.

practice.prompt: Say: I wash my hands before eating.
Negate with 안: 오늘은 운동을 해요.

lessons.culture: Korean libraries often mix quiet reading rooms with cafés and group study areas. 에서 tells a listener which kind of place you mean.

lessons.title: 오른쪽으로 가세요
lessons.summary: Ask for directions with movement verbs, direction particles, and polite requests.
goals: Say go to or come to a place
Give a direction with (으)로
Make a polite request with -(으)세요

grammar.title: Go to and come to
grammar.explanation: 에 marks the destination of movement verbs such as 가다 (go) and 오다 (come).
grammar.tip: The destination takes 에, not 에서.

grammar.title: Direction and method
grammar.explanation: (으)로 marks the direction of movement or the method used. Use 으로 after a consonant, 로 after a vowel, and 로 after ㄹ.
grammar.tip: For a method, (으)로 is like by or with. For a direction, it is like toward.

grammar.title: Polite request
grammar.explanation: Add -으세요 after a consonant stem and -세요 after a vowel stem to ask someone politely to do something. It is more polite than -아요/어요.
grammar.tip: This ending is also used for polite statements about someone older, not only requests. Stems ending in ㄹ drop it before 세요: 만들다 → 만드세요.

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: Excuse me. Where is the bank?

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.korean: 이 길로 쭉 가세요. 그리고 오른쪽으로 가세요.
dialogue.english: Go straight along this road. Then go to the right.

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: Is the hospital close too?

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.english: Yes, it is next to the bank.

practice.prompt: Say: I go to school.
Choose 으로 or 로: 오른쪽__ 가세요.
practice.answer: 으로, because 오른쪽 ends in a consonant.

practice.prompt: Make a polite request: 앉다.

lessons.culture: When asking for directions, use a landmark as well as a turn. 은행 옆 is often clearer than a street name, especially in dense neighborhoods.

chapters.title: 미래
chapters.summary: Make plans, explain reasons, and talk about what you want to do.
chapters.culture: Weekend and vacation plans are common conversation topics. Koreans often ask about a plan before suggesting a time or place.

lessons.title: 산책을 할 거예요
lessons.summary: Future plans, reasons with -아서/어서, and the ㅂ irregular.
goals: Use the ㅂ irregular
Give a reason with -아서/어서
State a future plan with -(으)ㄹ 거예요

grammar.title: ㅂ irregular
grammar.explanation: When a stem ends in ㅂ and the next ending begins with a vowel, ㅂ changes to 우. 돕다 and 곱다 are the exceptions and change to 오. 입다, 잡다, 씹다, and 좁다 stay regular.
grammar.tip: The ㅂ does not disappear. It becomes 우 and joins the ending.

grammar.title: Reason with -아서/어서
grammar.explanation: Attach -아서 after ㅏ or ㅗ and -어서 after other vowels to give a reason. 하다 verbs become 해서. The second clause is the result.

examples.english: It rained, so I stayed home.
I was tired, so I slept early.
The weather was good, so I took a walk.

grammar.tip: Do not use -아서/어서 with a command or suggestion in the second clause.

grammar.title: Future plan
grammar.explanation: Add -을 거예요 after a consonant stem and -ㄹ 거예요 after a vowel stem. It expresses a plan, intention, or prediction.
grammar.tip: This is a polite future form. The plain -겠습니다 is more formal and decisive.

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.english: What will you do on the weekend?

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: The weather will be good, so I will take a walk.

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.korean: 저는 방이 더러워서 청소를 할 거예요.
dialogue.english: My room is dirty, so I will clean it.

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.korean: 청소를 한 후에 같이 커피숍에 갈 거예요?
dialogue.english: After cleaning, will you go to a coffee shop together?

practice.prompt: Change to the polite present: 춥다.
Give a reason: 비가 와요. + 집에 있었어요.
Say: I will watch a movie.

lessons.culture: Weekend plans often depend on weather and housework. 청소 and 빨래 are common Saturday tasks, so they appear often in casual conversation.

lessons.title: 영화를 보려고 해요
lessons.englishTitle: I am going to see a movie
lessons.summary: Contrast with -지만, intentions with -(으)려고 해요, and the ㄷ irregular.
goals: Contrast two ideas with -지만
State an intention with -(으)려고 해요
Use the ㄷ irregular

grammar.title: Contrast with -지만
grammar.explanation: -지만 connects two clauses that contrast. The ending does not change for tense; the tense is shown on the verb before it.

examples.english: I like exercise but I do not do it often.

grammar.tip: -지만 is polite and neutral. It can also attach to past tense: 갔지만.

grammar.title: Intention
grammar.explanation: Add -으려고 해요 after a consonant stem and -려고 해요 after a vowel stem to say what you intend or plan to do.

examples.english: I am going to see a movie.
I am going to learn Korean.

grammar.tip: This focuses on the intention in your mind. -(으)ㄹ 거예요 can sound like a firmer plan. Stems ending in ㄹ drop the 으: 살다 → 살려고 해요.

grammar.title: ㄷ irregular
grammar.explanation: When a stem ends in ㄷ and the next ending begins with a vowel, ㄷ changes to ㄹ. 닫다, 받다, and 믿다 are regular and keep ㄷ.
grammar.tip: Check the next ending: only a vowel-initial ending triggers the change.

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: What are you going to do today?

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.english: I am going to exercise.

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: I am going to exercise too.

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.english: Good. Let's do it together.

practice.prompt: Contrast: 한국어는 어려워요. + 재미있어요.
Say: I am going to see a movie.
Change to polite present: 듣다.

lessons.culture: Koreans often state an intention before inviting someone. 같이 해요 after a plan is a friendly, low-pressure way to include the listener.

lessons.title: 여행을 가고 싶어요
lessons.summary: Talk about duration, conditions, and wishes.
goals: Say during or while with 동안
Make a condition with -(으)면
Express a wish with -고 싶다

grammar.title: During and while
grammar.explanation: 동안 means during a period. After a verb stem, -는 동안 means while doing something. The subjects of the two clauses can be the same or different.

examples.english: I will travel during the vacation.
I read a book while waiting.

grammar.tip: Use 동안 after a noun and -는 동안 after a verb.

grammar.title: If and when
grammar.explanation: Add -으면 after a consonant stem and -면 after a vowel stem. It marks a condition or a general when.

examples.english: If I have time, I will travel.
If it rains, I will stay home.
If you are tired, rest a little.

grammar.tip: The condition comes first. The result comes second. Stems ending in ㄹ drop the 으: 만들다 → 만들면.

grammar.title: Wanting to do
grammar.explanation: Add -고 싶다 to a verb stem to say I want to do it. For a third person, use -고 싶어하다.

examples.english: I want to go to Busan.
I want to see the sea.
My younger sibling wants to travel.

grammar.tip: The subject of -고 싶다 is normally the speaker, so it is usually I.

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: What will you do during the vacation?

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.english: I want to travel to Busan.

dialogue.speaker: 제인
dialogue.english: What do you want to do in Busan?

dialogue.speaker: 민호
dialogue.korean: 바다를 보고 맛있는 음식을 먹고 싶어요.
dialogue.english: I want to see the sea and eat good food.

practice.prompt: Say: I will travel during the vacation.
Make a condition: 시간이 있어요. + 여행을 갈 거예요.
Say: I want to go to Busan.

lessons.culture: Busan is a popular vacation choice for its beaches, markets, and slower pace. Summer train tickets sell out early, so plans are often made weeks ahead.
